title: Colonic diverticular hemorrhage associated with the use of nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs, low‐dose aspirin, antiplatelet drugs, and dual therapy

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>Background and Aim</jats:title><jats:p>The effects of various medications on lower gastrointestinal tract remains unknown. Here, we investigated the effects of nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s), low‐dose aspirin, and antiplatelet drugs associated with diverticular bleeding.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>This prospective study involved patients with diverticulosis who underwent colonoscopy. Alcohol and smoking, medications, and <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">C</jats:styled-content>harlson comorbidity index and <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">G</jats:styled-content>astrointestinal <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">S</jats:styled-content>ymptom <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">R</jats:styled-content>ating <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">S</jats:styled-content>cale scores were assessed. The medications evaluated were nine kinds of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s, two kinds of low‐dose aspirin, 10 kinds of nonaspirin antiplatelet drugs, three kinds of anticoagulants, acetaminophen, and corticosteroids. Adjusted odds ratios (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content>) were estimated by a logistic regression model.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>A total of 911 patients with non‐bleeding diverticula (<jats:italic>n</jats:italic> = 758) and bleeding diverticula (<jats:italic>n</jats:italic> = 153) were enrolled. Independent risk factors were alcohol consumption (light drinker, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 3.4; ≥ moderate drinker, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 3.3), smoking index (≥ 400, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 2.0), <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 4.6), low‐dose aspirin (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 1.9), and nonaspirin antiplatelet drugs (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 2.2). The drugs significantly associated with bleeding were loxoprofen (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 5.0), diclofenac (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 3.1), diclofenac suppository (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 8.0), etodolac (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 4.9), enteric‐coated aspirin (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 3.9), buffered aspirin (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 9.9), clopidogrel (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 2.5), and cilostazol (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 7.3). Dual therapy carried a higher risk than monotherapy (single <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 3.6, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.01; dual, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 23, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.01; single antiplatelet drug, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 2.0, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.01; dual, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">aOR</jats:styled-content> 4.1, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.01).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title><jats:p>Besides alcohol and smoking, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s, low‐dose aspirin, and antiplatelet drugs are risk factors for diverticular bleeding.
